So if a fringe moves 1/10 of a micron at 532, in what geometry would that help?

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **Johnfp:** I was with a holographer that swore a miiscule of fringe movement helped.So if a fringe moves 1/10 of a micron at 532, in what geometry would that help?In other words, do the finges need to be 50/50 albeit sinusoidul, but what happens if they sway a bit one way or another?

I'm not sure what you mean by "what geometry would that help?", but generally speaking, it's a rule of thumb that in transmission holograms you can "get away" with 1/2 lambda and with reflection you should aim for 1/4 lambda or less. Is this what you meant? Ideally, of course, you should have no overlap at all.

Generally, think of the hologram as a set of lines with a sinusoidal variation. You're trying to take a photograph of those lines. Like any photograph, if the subject moves, you get blurring. The diffraction from the lines, if perfect, will exactly reproduce one of the two waves that created the lines in the first place. However, if the lines have moved as you photographed them, then the blurred lines are not an exact replica. The fuzzier the replica, ie the more the motion, the worse is the diffraction. But, like any photograph, a slight motion doesn't matter. If a friend took you picture and you moved a little, your friend would still recognise you, if you moved so much that the whole,picture is blurred, your friend won't recognise you. 

How much is "too much"? It depends on the spatial frequency. The important point is that the actual motion is independent of the spatial frequency, and depends on the degree of motion. So, the lower the spatial frequency, then for a given motion, the less the deleterious effect.

So, let's say that the motion of a mirror or something causes a fringe shift of 1/2 a micron. In a transmission geometry with a HeNe at a reference angle of 30 degrees, the fringe separation is lambda/sin(theta) = 0.633/0.5 = 1.26 microns. A shift of 1/2 a micron is about 1/3 of a fringe separation (0.5/1.26 ~ 0.39) , leaving 2/3 of a fringe unaffected. You still have enough integrity as to not lose too much information. Now, shoot the same hologram in reflection with a ref at Brewsters. Now, the fringes are separated by 0.4 microns. Now a shift of 1 micron wipes out the entire fringe structure.

> **Johnfp:** I was with a holographer that swore a miiscule of fringe movement helped.

Not sure why anyone would say that. Tell your holographer to shake slightly next time he/she takes a picture of someone!

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: This might be sidestepping John's question, but fringe-lockers are usually considered to do their job when the fringe movement is kept within 1/20th of a fringe. I guess a fringe is defined as the distance from brightest to darkest?

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **Joe Farina:** I guess a fringe is defined as the distance from brightest to darkest?

No, one spatial wavelength of a fringe is defined as brightest to brightest or darkest to darkest, peak to peak or trough to trough. This is one complete wave of the sin function. This is what spatial frequency is based on. 

> **Joe Farina:** fringe-lockers are usually considered to do their job when the fringe movement is kept within 1/20th of a fringe.

No experience with fringe lockers. You mean that if the motion were greater than 1/20th of a fringe, the fringe locker would not be able to compensate? I've heard stories that people have literally stomped on the table during a shot and the fringe locker would compensate. I find this hard to believe unless the stomper stomped extremely slowly. I can't see how the fringe locker would compensate fast enough if the motion were extremely rapid. Also, if the fringe locker did compensate by, say, twisting a mirror, then wouldn't a fast response cause to mirror to overcompensate due to inertia and keep on moving when it should have stopped?

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
I'd say it depends on the recording material more than the geometry or spatial frequency of the system. Silver halide is very sensitive to fringe visibility. It takes very little light into the dark fringes to create latent image sites on the AgX crystals. Photopolymer is much less sensitive to fringe visibility, because it requires much more light to get molecules to cross link. Same with DCG. 

If there's 1/4 wave of motion during the exposure, fringe visibility decreases just the same as if the beam ratio was increased. If one has a system set up that gives optimum results at beam ratio of 10 with perfectly stable fringes, it may give optimum results at beam ratio of 2 in the presence of fringe motion that degrades fringe visibility to a point equal to that in the previous example (assuming there's no banding or other artifacts from what caused the fringes to move). Regardless, I agree with Dinesh that there's never any time when any fringe motion is better for a recording than no fringe motion. The entire technical goal of an optical holographer is to create a fringe pattern in space, and hold it still for an exposure.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Thanks Dinesh and Ed for clearing that up.

Dinesh, I'm surprised you haven't tried a fringe locker, because I think you would find it very interesting and maybe useful. There is a simple schematic on the Wiki which I wrote. It just uses a cheap op-amp that can be found at Radio Shack for about $1, a few resistors, two potentiometers, a cheap speaker, and two photodiodes or phototransistors. Anyway, it works very well to lock fringes. I stomp on the floor to see if it's working, if the fringes don't move, then it's working. As a matter of fact, I live one block from a railroad line that has two sets of tracks. Even when a single train goes by, the fringes often hold their lock. But when two trains go by at the same time, they are disrupted. When locked well, the fringes can hold their position for an undetermined amount of time, maybe an hour or more. The fringes look like they are painted on the wall, with no movement.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: Dinesh, I forgot that you asked about the 1/20th of a fringe thing. I think the idea is as follows. When a fringe-locker is used, if the gain on the op-amp is set fairly low (with the potentiometer), then it produces what's called a weak lock or a loose lock. The fringes drift very slightly (almost imperceptibly) but then the photodiodes sense the movement, and the system kind of "nudges" the fringes back into position. (A loose lock is not so good, because it can't compensate for vibrations very well either, and can easily lose the lock.) Anyway, I think this is the kind of movement that needs to be kept below 1/20th of a fringe, according to the literature I've read.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **Joe Farina:** Dinesh, I'm surprised you haven't tried a fringe locker, because I think you would find it very interesting and maybe useful.

Actually, a lot of people seem to be surprised. I just recently was working with a holographer and we had an unknown problem on the table. We eventually traced it to a laser umbilical touching the curtains surrounding the table. We did this by looking at a fringe locker output. So, he asked, "Are you now a convert to fringe lockers?" I had to admit I still wasn't!

I agree that if you're in a surround with heavy traffic, trains and so on, it would be a useful tool. However, luckily, I've never been in such a situation. The lab here in San Marcos, CA is in a light industrial park of mostly offices, so it's pretty quiet. There are occasional delivery trucks passing by, but the vibration isolation table seems to take care of them, so again not much of a problem. My "philosophy" is that the more components you load onto a system, the more failure modes you introduce and the more error prone is the system. So, basically, I like to keep things as simple and pared down as possible. Should I ever have occasion to work in a vibration prone environment, though, I probably would use a locker.

> **BobH:** If there's 1/4 wave of motion during the exposure, fringe visibility decreases just the same as if the beam ratio was increased.

I never actually thought about it like that, ie that fringe visibility is connected to ratio. Motion tends to smear out or flatten out the peak of the sinusoid because the peak shifts. Ratio determines the height of the sinusoid. So I suppose if there was a small flattening out of the sinusoid would have the same effect as lowering the peak of the sinusoid. 

Anyway, just out of curiosity, I did a quick back-of-an-envelope calculation. Here it is for anyone interested:

Motion causes a shift of the sinusoidal pattern. This is equivalent to adding a phase-shifted sinusoidal pattern to the original pattern. The sinusoidal pattern is actually a cos squared function. So, adding the original cos squared function to a phase shifted version of it results in:

Original pattern: (cos^2)(A) =(1/2)*(cos(2A) + 1)

Phase shifted pattern: (cos^2)(A + phi) = (1/2)*(cos(2(A+phi)) + 1)

Adding to give the final pattern on the plate: (1/2)*(cos(2A) + 1) + (1/2)*(cos(2(A+phi)) + 1) = (1/2)*(cos(2A) + cos(2A)cos(2phi) - sin(2A)sin(2phi)

If the motion is very small, phi is very small. In this case:

cos(2phi)~1 and sin(2phi) ~ 2phi

This gives: 2 cos(2A)/2 - 2(phi)sin(2A)

If you subtract the two, you get (1/2)cos(2A) _ (1/2) - 2phisin(2A) = (cos^2)(A) - 2(phi)sin(2A)

Giving you back the original pattern, with a small modulated sin wave sitting on top of the main sinusoidal fringe pattern.

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **BobH:** I'd say it depends on the recording material more than the geometry or spatial frequency of the system. Silver halide is very sensitive to fringe visibility. It takes very little light into the dark fringes to create latent image sites on the AgX crystals. Photopolymer is much less sensitive to fringe visibility, because it requires much more light to get molecules to cross link. Same with DCG.

That's an interesting observation. Maybe in a photopolymer system the fringe recording becomes kind of averaged over a relatively long period of time (involving extended diffusion processes during recording) compared to latent image formation in AgX.

Another thing in respect to fringe visibility not yet mentioned here might be the impact of the laser itself. Last year Ahmet and I made a test with his experimental ECDL. We shot one Denisyuk hologram on a piece of 8E75 film. Despite the poor cosmetic beam quality (cheap optics and no spatial filtering!) plus an object being placed at some 10cm from the recording plane, this was probably the brightest Denisyuk hologram I've ever seen on 8E75. Incidentally, this film was part of a batch I had bought from Agfa around 1993. While certain wines may mature, AgX materials usually don't become better over the years. So this amazing result clearly seems to be related to the laser. With my HeNe I've never produced anything alike.
